abstract.p: Green lab initiatives like My Green Lab and LEAF (Laboratory Efficiency Assessment Framework), are paving the way towards sustainable research by promoting resource efficiency, energy conservation, and waste reduction through behavioral changes. However, these initiatives focus almost exclusively on material consumption, overlooking deeper facets of scientific waste that stem from questionable research practices: the environmental cost of unnecessary or poorly designed experiments, discarded null results, unreproducible research, and distorted reporting. I argue that a more meaningful discussion of scientific sustainability must look beyond physical resource management to examine the scientific process itself; to rethink the questions we ask, the experiments we do, and how we communicate our findings. To build a truly sustainable scientific ecosystem, Green Lab initiatives must join forces with Open Science and research integrity movements to update not only the hardware, but also the software of science.

custom-meta.meta-value: To reduce the environmental footprint of scientific research, we must look beyond physical resource management and examine the deeper facets of scientific waste stemming from questionable research practices and distorted reporting.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: As much as scientific research offers unquestionable benefits for societal progress – including potential solutions to the climate crisis – the scientific process itself carries a significant environmental burden (Freese et al., 2024). Laboratory practices can be highly resource-intensive, contributing to greenhouse gas emissions, plastic waste, and toxic waste. Research laboratories produce an estimated 5.5 million tonnes of single-use plastic waste annually, accounting for 2% of the global total (Urbina et al., 2015), and typically consume 5–10 times more energy than standard office spaces (Kelly, 2023). That is why recent "Green Lab" initiatives, such as My Green Lab and LEAF (Laboratory Efficiency Assessment Framework), which aim to integrate sustainable practices into research, have come into the spotlight (My Green Lab - Education, 2026). But what do these projects really call for? And is it enough?

Green lab initiatives focus primarily on resource efficiency, energy conservation and waste reduction. They seek to reduce the environmental footprint of research by promoting behavioral changes such as limiting single-use plastics, turning off idle equipment, eliminating single-pass cooling systems, and implementing green chemistry principles (My Green Lab - Education, 2026, Freese et al., 2024). Crucially, however, these initiatives operate independently of the underlying research questions and attitudes toward scientific practice. As a result, they remain blind to vast layers of waste that have been steadily accumulating within the scientific ecosystem for decades.

When My Green Lab states that "laboratory waste could cover 57 square kilometers – 23 times the size of Manhattan – ankle deep," they are talking about physical, material waste – the kind of waste we would see if it covered our streets and feel as we wade through it. But statistics like these prompt a deeper question: What do we really consider ‘waste’ in research?

If an experimental breakthrough ends up saving thousands of lives, are the gloves used and discarded during that study waste? Is the water used to clean the beakers waste? And what about experiments conducted in energy-efficient labs that fail to reproduce, or that yield negative results that are never published? What about the animal lives used to manufacture an unpublishable p-value because the experimenter did not think to optimize their sample size? Evidently, any meaningful discussion of scientific sustainability must rethink the definition of waste – and rethink how we address it.

sec.title: Beyond green labs
sec.p: The movement toward sustainable science takes inspiration from circular economy principles: reduce, reuse, recycle, repair, and rethink. The last of these is probably the most neglected, but perhaps also the most impactful.

Working in biomedical research for several years, witnessing firsthand the wasteful practices that occur daily in the lab, I have come to realise that laboratory waste is not so much about the materials we use or when we turn off the lights. We need to talk about the larger facets of laboratory waste, and the gaping blind spots in how we as scientists think about sustainability.

Consider the three key stages that all research typically passes through: First, questions are formulated and decisions are made about which hypotheses will be tested. Second, experiments are designed and conducted, and data are collected and recorded. Finally, results are assessed, interpreted, and reported. Waste can occur at every stage of this pipeline, compounding as a project progresses. The quest for laboratory sustainability must therefore address waste at each phase.

sec.title: The questions we ask
sec.p: Sustainable science is about reducing the materials we use, but also the experiments we embark on in the first place. That does not mean that we should question less, but that we dwell more on which questions are worth answering – that we allocate more time and resources to refining our hypotheses and researching the state of the field, so that we can focus on the most likely impactful experimental tasks. It means finding out if an experiment has been done before by others before repeating it, stopping and considering whether it is possible to answer a question without doing further experiments – for example, by utilising publicly available datasets. Sustainable science means remembering the cold truth that the more efficient way to experiment is to not experiment – remembering that less experimentation does not equate to less discovery.

sec.title: The experiments we do
sec.p: Sustainable science means spending as much effort designing experiments as we do conducting them. It means optimizing sample sizes so that reagents, materials, human effort and animal lives are not wasted on unpublishable p-values. Sustainable science means maximizing the lifespan and utility of the models and data we produce rather than striving to produce more of them – treating these as reusable assets rather than disposable outputs. Sustainable science does not discard half of its animals because they are “complicated” (usually meaning female).

sec.title: The results we communicate
sec.p: Sustainable science needs transparency. It needs scientists who communicate exactly how experiments were done and who are open to sharing detailed methodologies, data, models and reagents – so that we do not have to keep reinventing the wheel. It needs willingness not only to communicate successes, but also failures – to share null results and ancillary findings, to accept non-significance and contradiction, and to value truth-telling over storytelling. Sustainable science does not discard half of its data because it is “negative”.

Hidden failures are a form of laboratory waste. Without open publication, scientists cannot know what hypotheses have already been tested, and what experiments have already been done. Unreported trials and hidden failures leave an open invitation for other researchers to follow the same rabbit holes, expending time, energy, material and financial resources and animal lives in the process.

At a global scale, duplicating hidden experiments is likely a multi-billion-euro inefficiency problem. A study from the European Commission in 2018 estimated that up to 26 billion euros were wasted in Europe due to duplicated work, owing to a lack of awareness of existing data or unreported results (Directorate-General for Research and Innovation and PwC EU Services, 2018). In another study from the US National Institute of Health, the cost to US taxpayers due to research waste and unreported trials was estimated as $100 million a year (Rees et al., 2023). Yet, alarmingly, this epidemic of null results has still not found its way into discussions of laboratory sustainability.

sec.title: Rethinking the software of science
sec.p: None of this is to diminish existing green lab initiatives. It is encouraging that programs like LEAF and My Green Lab exist, and that the scientific community is eager to adopt them. The current conversation is useful and important – but it will remain incomplete until we demand more of science than metaphorical paper straws and canvas bags. Does it not feel like we are simply "greening" a pipeline fundamentally designed to produce intellectual waste? Are we favoring dozens of useless experiments performed with "sustainable" methods over a few truly impactful studies that happened to use an extra plastic tube?

When we think about waste in the laboratory, we should think less about reusing pipette tips and the energy efficiency of our machines, and more about the larger facets of our scientific enterprise – the questions we ask, the quality of research design and methods, and the way we communicate findings. Because waste is choosing the wrong questions. Waste is doing studies that are unnecessary or poorly designed. Waste is keeping important aspects of research findings unpublished or publishing biased accounts. Waste is doing more while thinking less.

Effectively reducing the environmental footprint of scientific research requires systemic change. We won't achieve it solely by meticulously recycling pipette-tip boxes, any more than we can erase our personal carbon footprints by avoiding plastic straws. To achieve a truly sustainable scientific ecosystem, we must look beyond the physical laboratory walls and begin to update the "software" of science – we must think less about how we run the machine, and more about what we strive to achieve with it. In the end, if our work is not reproducible, credible, and useful, no amount of material greenwashing will make it sustainable.
